newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices tumble on news of Australian harvest.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices tumble on news of Australian harvest.

text.p: Wheat prices tumbled Tuesday on news that Australia was expected to harvest its second-largest crop ever.
Crude oil and gasoline prices rose as a strike at a French refinery entered its sixth day. Sugar prices fell after being under pressure from large world supplies.
Wheat prices have been falling since May and tumbled again recently when export business shifted to lower-priced foreign crops.

Adding to traders' woes, Australia's Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics, the country's official commodities forecaster, said the upcoming crop of 21.3 million metric tons would be the second largest after the 22 million tons harvested in 1984.

"There's no light at the end of the tunnel for the U.S. to sell wheat to anybody," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures. "There's a big Australian crop and they're going to have wheat left over. There's just no good news."
Also bearish for wheat was an Agriculture Department report on Monday stating that 75 percent of U.S. winter wheat crop was in good to excellent condition.

Soft red winter wheat for March delivery fell 5-1/4 cents to $3.72 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade. The December contract lost 8-1/4 cents to $3.85 a bushel, after 700,000 bushels were posted for delivery against that contract.
Kansas City Board of Trade March hard red winter wheat fell 4-1/2 cents to $3.88-1/2 a bushel and Minneapolis Grain Exchange March spring wheat dropped 7 cents to $3.73.

Crude oil futures recovered from early losses to close higher and gasoline posted strong gains for the second consecutive session, in reaction to strikes at three Elf Aquitaine refineries in France that have crippled French output.
"There is talk that gasoline imports which were heading over won't be because Europe now needs the supply," said a trader in New York.
Elf's workers entered their sixth day in the strike against the French oil giant, affecting 440,000 barrels a day in capacity.

"One hundred thousand barrels per day of gasoline production capacity in Europe is being shut off by the strike...It sounds small but we are living in a world of tight markets," said Peter Bogin, associate director of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
Also boosting gasoline's price was an explosion at a plant owned by Hoechst Celanese Corp in Texas. The plant makes a gasoline additive.

January gasoline rose 1.01 cents to 69.13 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. January crude oil added 13 cents to $24.93 a barrel and January heating oil gained 0.65 cent to 74.22 cents a gallon.
Fund selling pressured sugar prices sharply lower.
"This was purely technical. March failed to get over a previous high...hit stops and there were no buyers to buoy it up," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast.
"Fundamentally, reports of surplus production between 3 million and 7 million (metric) tons has been a burdening factor," Prendergast said.
German statistician F.O. Licht said on Friday that world sugar stocks may rise sharply from year-ago levels as output in major exporting nations is seen rising.
The March sugar contract fell 0.39 cent to 10.27 cents a pound at New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange.
